reporting-org.narrative: Defence for Children International Netherlands - ECPAT Netherlands

description.narrative: Sexual exploitation of children (SEC) is a grave violation of children’s rights and affects millions of children and youth annually, regardless of gender. No region, country or child is immune, though girls, boys and children with other gender identities face differing levels of risk to different manifestations of SEC depending on their intersectional vulnerability factors. It impacts heavily and long lastingly on their physical, emotional and mental well-being. It deprives children and youth of establishing healthy (sexual) relationships and from developing to the best of their potential.The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC and will work in 12 countries in Latin America and South and South East Asia: Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Philippines and Thailand.

The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC by working towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.” This activity forms part of the SUFASEC programme. The long-term impact will be reached through three interlinking objectives that address different dimensions (social norms, assets/environments, and laws/policies/systems).Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SECChildren and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environmentsChildren and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems

The different stakeholder groups involved in the SUFASEC programme include:Children and youth in all their diversity: A child-centred approach: children and youth are the most important stakeholders. When children/youth fall victim to SEC the physical and mental impact can be long lasting. The Alliance adheres to the UN definition of child (0-18 years) and youth (15-24 years)Caregivers and Communities: Critical stakeholders in the community include parents, caregivers, community leaders, teachers, local Community Based Organisations (CBOs), social workers, and other community members involved in community based child protection mechanisms.CSOs and CBOs: Local child protection organisations support and implement activities at community level, L&A towards national actors, and provide synergies of interventions.Local and national governments: formulate, endorse and implement laws and public policies related to SECPrivate Sector: Travel and tourism orgs (e.g., large and small, hotels, transport), as well as ICT/ Digital Service Providers have interest to avoid SEC taking place within their value chain, and to avoid having their products and services used to facilitate SECInternational donors, Intergovernmental bodies, INGOs, Multilateral entities55: Targeted audiences and partners for evidence based regional and international lobbyingDutch Stakeholders: NL Embassies in programme countries, MoFA, MoJ&S, to formalise the network for sustainable cooperation to end SEC and impunity of offenders. The Dutch PublicMedia & Journalists: Investigative and reporting outlets in the Programme countries. Media and journalists in the Netherlands.

title.narrative: Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved implementation of laws, policies, and systems
# of governmental policies blocked, adopted, improved leading to decrease of barriers to SRHR and HIV/AIDS services

comment.narrative: Currently, the Ministry of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection does not have any cooperation or Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with financial institutions such as PPATK (Indonesian Financial Transaction Reports and Analysis Center) and OJK (Financial Services Authority) to strengthen child protection efforts. In addition, OJK has not taken any specific measures to prevent or address child sexual exploitation and abuse (ESA) previously, despite being an institution with significant authority to influence financial service providers.

ECPAT Indonesia will encourage the Ministry of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (KemenPPPA), PPATK (Financial Transaction Reports and Analysis Center), and OJK (Financial Services Authority) to establish a cooperation agreement aimed at enhancing child protection efforts, particularly in how they can be more progressive in preventing and responding to the misuse of financial service providers for transactions related to child sexual exploitation and abuse CSEA. Additionally, ECPAT Indonesia will advocate for OJK's involvement in efforts to prevent and address CSEA.

MoWEaCP has facilitated a Child Safeguarding Coordination Meeting to enhance collaboration with the financial sector. Additionally, they have allocated their Assistant Deputy to collaborate with ECPAT for DtZ program activities. MoWEaCP has also initiated the development of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with PPATK, BI, and OJK.OJK has been involved in mobilizing financial service providers to engage on SEC issues through Multi-stakeholder meeting and ECPAT research activities. They have also provided input for the quick research report.

comment.narrative: Since we are looking at people reached with information given by SUFASEC during programme, we set this baseline value as zero. CSOs have not yet recognized how financial service providers can play a role in combating SEC. In Indonesia, there hasn't been an advocacy network specifically addressing this issue. While there are CSO networks focused on child online protection or child labor, they do not currently engage the financial sector in responding to SEC.
Engage with CSOs to develop research on the misuse of financial service providers for transactions related to SEC

ECPAT Indonesia continue working with the same children from Year 1. However, we provide training on different topics, including OCSEA and SRHR. We select children and youth who demonstrate leadership skills, effective public speaking, and involvement in community organizations. Our goal is to build their capacity, empower them as peer educators, and support them in developing action plans for their communities. To involve children with diverse gender identities and marginalised children

In Year 3, a total of 63 young people (39 female, 21 male, and 3 identifying as other), aged 15–24, were strengthened over the three-year period, demonstrating increased knowledge and the ability to disseminate information on CSE, SEC, and SRHR through KOMPAK Jakarta and YVFC (ECPAT Indonesia Youth Group).In YEAR 3, SEC was delivered through both in-school and out-of-school approaches, including innovative methods such as creative mini-theater and peer-led training sessions. The mini-theater addressed various forms of SEC, SRHR topics, and access to services, reaching 250 young people as well as 50 teachers, parents, and other stakeholders. Infographics and digital brochures were also developed, printed, and disseminated by yvfc member to raise awareness of online SEC and provide information on available helplines. In addition, yvfc member facilitated sessions for student council members on online SEC, including reporting and response mechanisms, as well as digital literacy through the CTRL Youth training program.A Boys’ Initiative was implemented by KOMPAK Jakarta and YVFC members to challenge harmful gender norms that discourage boys from speaking up about violence and sexual exploitation, reaching 200 young people. The Boys’ Initiative module, developed by the KOMPAK Jakarta serves as a training tool for selected student representatives from partner schools, equipping them to further promote and disseminate key messages related to the initiative. Awareness-raising stickers were also designed and produced by KOMPAK Jakarta to promote better understanding of boys’ protection issues.Additionally, participants engage in Boys Initiative event produced creative outputs as part of the learning process, including poster, stand-up comedy performances, and a YouTube video created by a girl focusing on male empowerment. The video challenges gender stereotypes and encourages boys to reflect on emotional expression and equality.

we have already reached out to LGBT and transgender organizations to involve their youth groups in our training. title.narrative: # of young people (male) reached with comprehensive, correct information on sexuality, HIV/AIDS, STIs, pregnancy and contraception

comment.narrative: Since we are looking at people reached with information given by SUFASEC during programme, we set this baseline value as zero. This indicator includes young people reached with information on SEC (and not only SRH). There are still children who are unaware of the various forms of sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA), despite several children having been victims. Out of 31 children and youth surveyed, 10 have never reported being victims of SEA or other violence.

Capacity-building for youth leaders aged 13-24 years old will focus on understanding the forms on SEC and not only SRH, current trends, reporting channels, and youth-led advocacy. Additionally, they will receive essential knowledge about their rights and gender concepts to prevent sexual violence.

Capacity-building activities for children and youth leaders aimed at preventing the sexual exploitation of children.Participants were selected based on their concern for child protection and leadership skills, which they will become champions or peer educators in preventing SEC in their regions. The activities included:This capacity-building session covered topics such as Child Rights in the Convention on Children's Rights and the Legal Framework in Indonesia, Sexual Exploitation of Children, Gender Concepts, and Youth-Led Advocacy.In-Depth Class to Deep Dive into SEC Issue Trends involving AI and Financial Service Providers: This session delved into emerging trends in sexual exploitation of children, including issues involving artificial intelligence (AI) and financial service providers. The class also addressed advocacy activities that children and youth can initiate and participate in.These capacity-building activities reached 61 youths and children aged 14-23 years old from 18 provinces through offline and online channels.Through this capacity-building initiative, children and youth leaders demonstrated an increase in their knowledge regarding various forms of violence and sexual exploitation of children, particularly those occurring online. children and young people mentioned receiving detailed information about child sexual exploitation, enabling them to understand their roles and the actions that could be taken when encountering such cases. In the coming years (Year I and II), we plan to enhance the capacity of these children and youth leaders on various issues related to sexual exploitation of children, including Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR), and other relevant topics to strengthen their advocacy actions. we will also conduct monitoring to assess the follow-up actions that they plan during the sessions. In addition, we will engage more youth with divers gender identitiy.

To involve children with diverse gender identities, we will reach out to adults in partner organizations to help us engage with these children and youth.
